reference.source: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
clinicalPearls: A deep neck space infection with pus collecting between the posterior pharyngeal wall and the prevertebral fascia, most often in young children

The acute form in children usually follows suppuration of retropharyngeal lymph nodes after an upper respiratory infection, whereas a chronic form can result from tuberculous disease of the cervical spine
Typical features are fever, dysphagia, drooling, refusal of feeds, a muffled cry, neck stiffness, and the child holding the neck extended
Examination may show a bulge on one side of the posterior pharyngeal wall, and stridor or respiratory difficulty signals airway threat
A lateral soft-tissue neck radiograph classically shows widening of the prevertebral soft tissue, and contrast computed tomography defines the abscess and its extent
Management combines securing the airway, intravenous antibiotics, and surgical drainage of the collection, with drainage usually via the transoral route in the acute form
The infection can spread inferiorly into the mediastinum along fascial planes, which is a dangerous complication
Chronic (tuberculous) retropharyngeal abscess presents more insidiously and is drained by an external approach rather than transorally
reference.pathophysiology: The retropharyngeal space lies between the buccopharyngeal fascia covering the pharynx and the prevertebral fascia, and contains lymph nodes that drain the nasopharynx, adenoids, and posterior nasal structures. In young children an upper respiratory infection can seed these nodes, which suppurate to form an acute abscess; these nodes largely regress with age, making the acute form rare in adults, where trauma or foreign body is more often responsible. The chronic form arises from caries of the cervical vertebrae (Pott disease), where tuberculous pus tracks forward into the space. Because the space communicates inferiorly with the mediastinum, infection can descend to cause mediastinitis.
additionalDifferentials: Prevertebral or vertebral tuberculosis without abscess
additionalInvestigations: Lateral soft-tissue neck radiograph to detect prevertebral soft-tissue widening
Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the neck to confirm the abscess and assess spread toward the mediastinum
Full blood count and inflammatory markers to gauge severity
Blood cultures and pus culture at drainage to guide antibiotic therapy
Investigations for tuberculosis and spinal imaging when a chronic abscess is suspected
redFlags: Stridor, drooling, or respiratory distress indicating airway compromise that demands urgent airway management
Rapid spread with signs of descending mediastinitis such as chest pain and sepsis
Torticollis with neurological signs suggesting cervical spine involvement
Sepsis or vascular complications such as jugular vein thrombosis
reference.prognosis: With prompt airway protection, appropriate antibiotics, and timely surgical drainage the acute abscess resolves well in most children; delay can lead to airway obstruction, aspiration on rupture, or life-threatening mediastinitis, and the chronic tuberculous form requires prolonged antitubercular treatment alongside drainage.
pitfalls: Failing to anticipate and secure a threatened airway before other interventions
Attempting transoral drainage of a chronic tuberculous abscess instead of an external approach
Missing downward spread into the mediastinum
Overlooking underlying cervical spine tuberculosis in an insidious presentation
references: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
management: Secure and protect the airway as the immediate priority, with intubation or, rarely, tracheostomy if the airway is threatened
Start empirical broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics covering streptococci, staphylococci and oral anaerobes, such as a beta-lactam with beta-lactamase inhibitor or clindamycin
Undertake surgical drainage of the collection, usually by the transoral route in the acute form
De-escalate to targeted antibiotic therapy guided by pus and blood culture results
Provide supportive care with intravenous fluids and analgesia during the acute illness
Monitor for complications, particularly descending mediastinitis, aspiration on rupture and airway obstruction
Investigate for and treat tuberculosis with antitubercular therapy when a chronic cold abscess from cervical spine disease is suspected
